institutionName: University of Natural Resources and Life Sciences, Vienna (BOKU)

questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Firstly that it was a good university (rankings etc.) with some really interesting angles on/focus areas with regards to my areas of interest in my academic field. Secondly it also mattered to me that Vienna seemed like a super interesting city with lots to explore.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: You have to be ready to spend quite some time on bureaucracy/paperwork. But apart from that, it was really really great (and definitely worth it)

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy, BOKU is quite structured with providing checlists and information meetings about nearly everything (which is also crucial because their system is in some ways very different from that of UCPH)

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: In addition to all the information meetings, the international office as well as the coordinators for my specific programme were always very helpful.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
A lot easier than in Copenhagen!! I just found my housing through another international student, but a lot of people used
www.WG-gesucht.de
, which is free and kinda like "Boligportalen" in Denmark, or some of the multiple facebook groups for housing in Vienna (look out for scammers though) or for international students etc. in Vienna, where people also often put up their flats/rooms when leaving the city.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: There seems to be a lot of student dorms in Vienna (a list can be found on the BOKU homepage), but not really any on campus, so everybody will be living off campus in one way or another. BOKU has two different campuses in Vienna (Peter Jordan-Strasse and Muthgasse) , so it might be a nice idea to check before arriving where your main insitute/the majority of your classes will be, if you want to live in a convenient distance. On the other hand, most of the social things takes place at the Peter Jordan campus, so living in a manageable distance to that might always be nice.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: As mentioned, I found my housing fast through an aquaintance, so I was never really on the real housing market, so I don't know if I am really the right one to judge it. But what is above is my general secondhand imperession.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The system is actually quite nice and flexible, but just very different from UCPH so at first it can be quite confusing. There's a lot less rules and deadlines, and a lot more free choice and stamps :-)

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
You first have to register preliminarily online some time before 
arriving (you get an e-mail about this), and later you have to book an 
appointment online for in-person registration at the study services at the main campus. Thereafter you get your student login and student card, and is able to register for classes etc.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer:
The International Office at BOKU is there to help, and the BOKU 
Study Services themselves are also very helpful

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got all the classes I wanted, not all in the first try but because the system at BOKU is quite different from UCPH: in most classes the deadline for deregistration (which is individual for each class) is a couple of weeks or more into the course, and even if you don't deregister you will not have to take the exam, then you just don't get the ECTS – and you can take all the classes you want, no matter ECTS, and also go to all the exams, then you just have to pick which ones you want on your transcript. Because of this, most students register for more classes in the beginning of semester than they intend on taking, and then they check them out in the first couple of lectures and decide which ones they're gonna keep. So even if you are still on waiting list for a course you really want at semester start you can just ask the professor if it its ok that you attend anyway, and then you'll probably end up getting a registered spot during the first week or so (unless the class is extremely popular and you're super far down the waiting list, but then the professor will tell you that).

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I would say that it's pretty much the same as at UCPH. Most classes are fewer ECTS though, so in that way they're of course lighter and often more narrow/focused, but then there's more of them. The field excursion courses are often easier (not all of them though), but then you have to be ready for spending days in row away, and often also paying yourself for transport etc (but it's definitely worth it, you can get to see some amazing places).

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: That actually differed a lot to me. Some classes were a lot more traditional/conservative lecture style than at UCPH, but then at the other hand some were far more experimental and interactive. There's a really broad scope, maybe it also depends a bit on the department (although I don't really know) That is also definitely one of the things where it is so great that you can try the classes out, and if the teaching style doesn't work for you, you can just deregister.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 2 semesters

questions.answer:

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I think most of my classes were really great but these 2 definitely stood out to me:

934002 Gender, food systems and natural resources: This is one of the best university classes I've ever had.  It was 3 intense weeks in what is actually the university holiday between semesters, very interactive teaching style, about as the name says natural resources and food systems and the way these are accessible or not to people and cultures, and how we use them and how we see them, and the role of gender in it all, but also about different kinds of research. For me as a very clear natural science student it really put everything into new systems and perspective for me, and the lecturer Stephanie Lemke is amazing. And it doesn't matter if you know anything about this beforehand, people have all sorts of different academic fields and focuses at this course. You just have to be reasy for 2-3 really intense weeks, but it is so worth it. 
833317 Formulation of questions and experimental design in ecological 
research: On paper a somewhat introductory statistics class. The curriculum is quite classic biology/natural science statistics I guess but the lecturer Marcela is amazing at her stuff, so even though I've had some statistics before I felt like a learned a lot of new things, and the things I'd had in other classes before, I actually really LEARNED here, if that makes sense. I think everybody should take this class it is such a good investment, especially for your thesis and stuff like that. And it is actually really fun and manageable!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer:
There were a few smaller fees for registering Vienna, for the Student Union 
(compulsory) at BOKU, and for a few excursions (not compulsory, depending 
on classes). All of these were around 20 euro each, as I remember.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Most prices are very similar to Danish prices, eating out is a bit cheaper. In 
contrast to at UCPH, I didn't spend any money on study books - everything 
was provided as PDFs (I don't know if this is a general thing, though).

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
A lot of clubs and events and friday bars and volunteer opportunities in the 
environmental/agricultural area. Crucial to mention here is that I was on exchange during 
lockdown, so I did not get the full picture of this, but I definitely got the impression that the social part of university life is very important to BOKU and therefore very well supported - a lot of possibilities.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
I was a volunteer at the BOKU garden, which is a "wild" utility garden driven 
by BOKU students at the outskirts of Vienna. Super cosy, great people, and 
a really nice break from studying/city life. Apart from that, meet the locals by going to the friday bars, the concert, the "stammtisches" (cosy meetings at bars), everything. There's plenty to choose from!
(Kinda academically, but still not directly part of "school") it is often possible to volunteer or just get student access at some of the many (!) interesting seminars hosted by BOKU and that way get to experience some really interesting talks and excursions.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Do a Stadtwanderweg (local hiking routes) in the nearby mountains, visit the 
opera, or one of the many many museums, go for a swim in the Donau, or get cheap standing tickets for one of the operas. See if there's a funny/interesting festival going on. There's always SO much to do in Vienna. 
don't even know, there's so much to do in Vienna. Or

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Coming from Denmark it was quite easy. Sometimes things were a bit more formal, especially at university, but apart from getting used to that it was very easy to adjust.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Go to many social events at BOKU, maybe get a hobby like taking dance classes or join the Boku garden or something. Some say that Austrians are quite distanced/hard to befriend, but I didn't find it much different than Denmark (which has the same reputation, to be fair), so you need a bit of stubbornness in making new local friendships but it is definitely possible (and worth it)

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The culture is a bit more formal generally, with more use of titles (such as Dr etc) and courteous expressions so coming from very direct/informal Denmark it might be a good idea to really be conscious about acting politely(not that the difference from Denmark is that big, but it is the only thing I would say sometimes could be a bit challenging or just different)

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Vienna is just a sprawling, cultural city, with such a rich, culturally mixed (and also very tragic of course) history, that is in some ways very different from the rest of Austria, it seems - and also in some ways very Austrian of course. It is just a lot, in the very best sense.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Be prepared for some time-consuming bureaucracy, it is worth it. 
2. You will definitely get some academic (and cultural) experiences that you can not get at UCPH. Enjoy that. Take advantage of the freedom in choosing and dropping courses to explore new fields and angles. 
3. Don't get scared away by the rumoured "coldness" of Viennese people. It is really not that different from Denmark.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Just again - everything I've written here has also been from a lockdown perspective, so maybe some things are quite different when not in lockdown, I don't know.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Actually just studying natural/environmental science in a country with such a different hsitory, location, climate, geography etc. than Denmark was so rewarding, and really gave me a new perspective on many things.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Lockdown. Haha. Apart from that, it is of course tough at times to be away from everything you know, always dealing with new systems that you don't understand. I think it is for everybody, that should not be a secret. But you learn so much from it as well, and it is worth it.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
